installation.note: chmod is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: chmod (change mode) modifies file and directory permissions. Linux uses a permission system with three types of access (read, write, execute) for three categories of users (owner, group, others). chmod is essential for file security and access control.

syntax.description: Change permissions of FILE(s) to MODE. MODE can be numeric (755) or symbolic (u+x).

misconceptions.title: chmod 777 is safe
misconceptions.misconception: Giving everyone all permissions (777) is fine
misconceptions.reality: chmod 777 gives read, write, and execute to everyone - this is a security risk. Only use when absolutely necessary (like /tmp).
misconceptions.tip: Avoid 777. Use 755 for executables, 644 for files, 750 for private directories.

misconceptions.title: chmod only works on files
misconceptions.reality: chmod works on both files and directories. Directory permissions control access to list contents (read) and create files (write).
misconceptions.tip: Directories need execute permission to be entered. Use chmod +x directory to allow access.

common_pitfalls.description: Giving everyone all permissions when not needed
common_pitfalls.solution: Use appropriate permissions: 755 for executables, 644 for files, 750 for private. Only use 777 for temporary directories like /tmp.

common_pitfalls.description: Only changing directory permissions, not contents
common_pitfalls.solution: Use chmod -R to apply permissions recursively to directory contents. Be careful - affects all files.

common_pitfalls.description: Removing own permissions (chmod 000) and losing access
common_pitfalls.solution: If you lock yourself out, use sudo chmod to restore permissions, or ask administrator for help.

best_practices: Use 755 for executables (owner: rwx, others: rx)
Use 644 for regular files (owner: rw, others: r)
Use 750 for private directories (owner: rwx, group: rx)
Use symbolic notation (u+x) for readability when adding/removing
Use numeric notation (755) for setting exact permissions
Use chmod -R carefully - affects all files recursively
Check permissions with ls -l before and after chmod
performance_tips: chmod -R can be slow on large directory trees
Use -v flag to see progress on recursive operations

additional_notes.permission_bits: Permissions: r=4 (read), w=2 (write), x=1 (execute). Add numbers: 7=r+w+x, 5=r+x, 4=r only
additional_notes.symbolic_notation: Symbolic: u=user, g=group, o=others, a=all. Operators: +=add, -=remove, ==set
additional_notes.directory_permissions: Directories need execute (x) permission to be entered. Read (r) allows listing contents.
additional_notes.security: Principle of least privilege - give minimum permissions needed. Avoid 777 unless necessary.
